of young children and immunocompromised individuals. Notwithstanding a propensity
for human diagnostic error, visual inspection is still predominantly utilized
for clinical diagnoses. Previous studies exploring the application of computer-
aided intestinal parasite classification have faced challenges due to the visual
similarities between parasites and other contaminants in fecal matter. This
paper introduces Deep Belief Networks as a solution to the challenges faced by
computer-aided intestinal parasite classification, showcasing the successful
application of DBNs on a dataset of 871 images containing three species of
intestinal parasites, which yielded an accuracy of 92.9% in classification.

This work introduces a novel approximation technique for a broad category of zero-sum-free stochastic differential investment and reinsurance models. It incorporates both proportional reinsurance and loss-overlimit reinsurance models. To calculate the Nash equilibrium, a Markov chain approximation approach and a dynamical programming technique are used to solve nonlinear integro-differential Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs equations. In addition, the research shows the convergence of the approximating sequences to the accurate solution of the value functions, which is supported by several numerical case studies.

This research presents a novel Proportional-Integral-Derivative-Accelerated (PIDA) control strategy, integrating a derivative filter, to enhance quadcopter stability in chaotic and unpredictable flight conditions. The mathematical framework is established based on a highly accurate model that effectively simulates a quadcopter's dynamic behavior. To assess the proposed controller's performance, a Stochastic Dual Simplex Algorithm (SDSA) is utilized for tuning the PIDA controller's parameters. Furthermore, a Genetic Filter is applied to improve the filter's performance by genetically optimizing its key configuration parameters. The outcomes indicate that the SDSA-predictive control approach leads to notable improvements in flight smoothness using the proposed PIDA control strategy.

A comprehensive examination of pion-nucleon interactions at low energy is provided,
with the intention of offering a fundamental and educational overview relevant to current
research endeavors. Key topics addressed include the application of chiral effective
field theory, the significance of the sigma term, an understanding of the qualitative nature
of low-energy phase shifts, the physics governing the $\Delta$ resonance, and isospin violation.
It is emphasized that pion-nucleon scattering at low energy can be poorly described by Born terms, 
as this regime falls outside this approximation's validity. Furthermore, the implications of the 
EM mass splittings between nucleon states with and without pions are explored.

The Compact Muon Solenoid (CMS) is one of the primary detectors in the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) at CERN, tracking particle interactions resulting from high-energy collisions. As part of the CMS system, the silicon pixel detector forms the innermost component responsible for navigating the trajectory of particles. Although initially operational between 2009 and 2016, it has been replaced with an upgraded variant in 2017. During a preceding period of shutdown for the LHC, an upgraded forward pixel detector prototype featuring a novel readout system and third disk was introduced, integrating eight pilot blades built using advanced digital readout chips. These pilot blades contained 16 individual strips with sensors reading different data and rotated 20.37 degrees relative to one another. A specific type of particle, known as secondary muon ions, generated at the LHC's proton beam collision energies, was used for testing purposes. As the particle tracks are highly curved and offer precise kinematic information, they proved to be an effective candidate for testing the new forward pixel detector prototype. The pilot blade's performance was evaluated by analyzing the efficiency of hit finding and tracking. The results indicate that the production pilot blade functions efficiently, with results comparable to the established forward pixel detector concepts in CMS. Furthermore, the investigation revealed minimal single-hit ambiguities, with the majority occurring due to data corruption from the digital readout chip. Consequently, the ambiguity impact on the pilot blade's functionality is thought to be marginal.

We have developed a machine learning algorithm capable of identifying and categorizing galaxy hosts for active nuclei up to a redshift of $z=1$. This algorithm was trained using approximately 1,000 galaxies from the Hyper Suprime-Cam survey with redshifts between 0.1 and 1, and has been validated on 844 galaxies from the same dataset. We used morphological classifications derived from exponential and Sersic fits to develop three host galaxy types: early-type, late-type, and irregular galaxies. Our test showed that the machine learning algorithm accurately classified early and late types in 85% and 75% of cases, respectively, and irregularly shaped galaxies in 60% of cases. This classification framework is expected to facilitate future studies using the Hyper Suprime-Cam survey, including determining the relationships between active nuclei host galaxies and their properties.

High-energy and high-momentum fluctuations occur within the nucleus due to short-range correlations. In order to understand how these correlations affect the nucleus's bulk properties, it's necessary to study their spatial distribution, which will help clarify their relationship between the coordinate and momentum spaces. Employing the lowest-order correlation operator approximation, the distribution of short-range correlations in both the nucleus's density and the Wigner distribution are examined for different nuclei. It's found that short-range correlations contribute nearly the same amount to the nucleus's density as its kinetic energy density. Furthermore, the spatial distribution of correlations for different nuclei follows a similar pattern to the nucleus's mean square radius, which was found in previous research. In momentum space, the correlations account for a relatively small fraction of the nucleus's total momentum distribution. It's observed that the distribution of correlations in momentum space exhibits symmetry and the magnitude of the diagonal terms is substantially greater than the off-diagonal terms. This study demonstrates that short-range correlations have a minimal impact on the nucleus's total momentum distribution but significantly affect the nucleus's density. In addition, this investigation highlights the distinct characteristics of short-range correlations in both the momentum and coordinate spaces, which will facilitate future research on this topic.

We are studying complex scaling as an inherent property unique to complex number systems and its applications. By extending the complex domain without considering complex scaling, Deep Complex Networks (DCN) is limited, whereas SurReal achieves scaling invariance but discards complex information. In contrast, we approach complex scaling as a distinct co-domain transformation and create neural network functions tailored for this unique operation. Furthermore, we propose innovative complex-valued representations of RGB images where scaling indicates changes in color hue and color intensity across different pixels. Compared to DCN and SurReal on datasets MSTAR, CIFAR10, CIFAR100, and SVHN, our co-domain symmetric classifiers exhibit enhanced accuracy, improved generalizability, increased robustness, reduced bias and variance with significantly fewer parameters.

The non-linear QCD evolution equations ultimately lead to the saturation of gluon distribution.  When gluon distribution becomes saturated, it establishes a distinct gluon density threshold per unit rapidity per transverse area known as the saturation momentum.  In certain large-energy situations within specified kinematic domains, saturation momentum becomes the only determining factor in physical processes. Consequently, a variety of observable outcomes display characteristic patterns of geometrical scaling. Several illustrations of such scaling patterns can be seen in various reactions.

A thorough understanding of the composition of early galaxies and the co-evolution of dwarf galaxies and their central black holes remains a persistent puzzle. Although, theoretically, the spread in metal abundance around low-mass early galaxies should provide valuable insights to this effect, the initial data did not show any significant dispersion, likely due to a lack of detailed abundance data. We've compiled a dataset with detailed abundance information for 16 central stars in five low-mass galaxies, allowing us to investigate whether galactic metallicity varies significantly. Contrary to expectations, we've observed significant dispersion in the abundance of one galaxy, but not in the other systems. Furthermore, we've established that variations in star formation rates or timescales could contribute to the abundance dispersion, which is consistent with the hypothesis that satellite galaxies accreted to our current galaxy (the Milky Way) may have had pre-accretion metallicity values that were relatively uniform.

A novel machine learning approach has been developed to quantify the influence of individual observations on predictive models. This framework enables data analysts to identify which data points have the greatest impact on accuracy and predictability, providing opportunities for optimization and improved model performance. The theoretical basis for this approach lies in advanced mathematical concepts, specifically operator theory and the derivation of influence functions from these principles. Experimental validation has been conducted, along with a case study examining financial literacy as a predictive factor in stock market involvement.

This research introduces SQUID, an open-source tool for developing and training hybrid Quantum-Classical classification algorithms. It utilizes PyTorch for the classical components, allowing for the creation of multiple quantum models that can be optimized with back-propagation. We demonstrate SQUID's capabilities by showcasing its implementation in a standard binary classification task from the widely-used MNIST dataset. Notably, we discuss how the choice of output affects the scalability of quantum models when utilizing gradient-based optimization.

Researchers, Chen and Garay, have examined pointwise slant submanifolds in almost Hermitian manifolds. By extending the concept of slant submanifolds to semi-slant ones, this study delves into their geometry in both Sasakian and cosymplectic manifolds. Key findings indicate a limitation on semi-slant warped products in Sasakian manifolds. On the other hand, non-trivial semi-slant warped products have been discovered in cosymplectic manifolds, and several foundational results have been obtained, including a defining characteristic of such semi-slant warped products.

The PALEOCCENE concept has the potential to develop sensitive and efficient low-energy detectors that can operate at room temperature and are minimally maintained. Such detectors could range in weight from grams to kilograms and could detect nuclear recoil events triggered by various factors including neutron scattering, CEvNS, or interactions with dark matter. Ongoing research, including existing and planned studies, is being conducted to explore the practicality of this technique for multiple applications.

We examine a rigid structure composed of two active Brownian particles that interact in a potential with a shallow well, positioned within a spatially varying activity field. Our investigation focuses on the influence of this external agent on the structural and dynamic properties of the forming dimer. Via non-equilibrium dynamic Monte Carlo simulations, we assess and quantify the effect of the activity gradient on monomer and dimer formation, breaking rates, and related coagulation mechanisms. Notably, our results indicate that the activity gradient can both expedite and hinder dimer formation, primarily due to its influence on the interaction between colloid particles and the dynamic self-correlation of the system. Furthermore, the activity gradient is found to modulate the collision mechanism, particularly in the direction of fastest movement of the colloid particles, leading to a significant increase in coagulation kinetics. These findings have significant implications for the study of colloidal systems in varied and dynamic environments.

We investigate numerically charge-neutral collective excitations in fractional quantum Hall systems, focusing on two specific Jain states, ν=2/7 and ν=2/9 near quarter filling, and the 1/4 Fermi-liquid state, contrasting them with the behavior observed in 1/3 states and those near half filling. Unlike those latter states, each 2 n /3 state (with n = 1,2,3,4) exhibits multiple magnetoroton spectral peaks around its ground state, this phenomenon is characterized through the ground state projection method, and its origin can be traced to an interesting sum rule.

Epidemics on massive contact networks with millions of individuals pose significant challenges for analysis and containment due to their immense scale. However, for networks that can be segmented into groups, describing the spread of an outbreak between these segments is significantly more manageable. Typically, studies have relied on dividing individuals into equitable subgroups to simplify the analysis, but a more inclusive approach is possible. Focusing on SIS epidemics, we offer three key contributions: Firstly, we present a geometric approach to determine which networks facilitate outbreaks between limited clusters. Secondly, we develop an efficient algorithm to identify the most effective contact subalgebra for calculating epidemic dynamics within multiple segments. Lastly, we provide arguments supporting the algorithm's suppression and convergence. This method outperforms existing hierarchical and non-equitable clustering approaches in scalability, especially for large datasets. For instance, processing a 2 million individual network takes only 0.02 seconds on a standard computer.

The maximum likelihood estimator used in CMB map-making provides optimal, unbiased results as long as the underlying data model is accurate, but inaccuracies often arise due to sub-pixel structures, instrumentation flaws such as time-varying gain and pointing errors, leading to model inaccuracy in practice. When errors occur, this estimator becomes biased, causing distortions to spread across the scan plane through sampling correlations in the data. In particular, pointing errors resulting from telescope pointing defects can cause 'X' shapes when sampling around strong point sources, leading to distorted parameter estimations for sources and systematic errors. To combat this issue, we have developed a method of cross-correlation whitening to mitigate the effects of sampling distortions between scanning patterns, demonstrating its effectiveness in reducing distortion spread and source parameter bias.

Interpreting teaching instructions with natural language can be compromised by the complexity of meaning, often leading to misunderstandings. Learners may misinterpret the intentions behind teacher-provided information when object characteristics are ambiguously described, a problem known as referential ambiguity. We explore how principles from cognitive sciences, such as teaching strategies (tailoring instructions) and adapting to agent preferences, can mitigate referential ambiguities through induction. Our experiments involve training two artificial agents to accomplish a simulated robotic task (block-stacking) and demonstrate that incorporating these ideas increases the learner's sample efficiency.

Quantum process tomography is crucial for building quantum computers, establishing quantum networks, and developing quantum sensors. Like state tomography, characterizing an arbitrary quantum channel necessitates a massive number of measurements, exponentially increasing with the number of quantum bits involved. Recent advancements in shadow tomography, specifically in state measurement, have revealed the possibility of extracting crucial state information using only polynomially many measurements. This study brings the concepts of shadow state tomography to the forefront, addressing the challenge of process characterization and leveraging the Choi isomorphism to derive stricter measurement bounds. Additionally, the research provides exclusive bounds applicable solely to process tomography, along with novel algorithms for its implementation, ultimately leading to new techniques, including channel concatenation and state channel applications. This breakthrough facilitates a significant improvement in understanding large-scale quantum systems.

We aim to derive precise bounds for the Cheeger constant using a range of geometric attributes such as area, perimeter, inradius, circumradius, minimum width and diameter. Our approach involves establishing tight inequalities among these measures specifically for planar convex bodies, along with formulating new conjectures that stem from numerical experiments.

This study investigates the optimal flight path for a drone to follow when transporting cargo that must be delivered within a set time frame in order to avoid incurring waiting fees. The path is based on a 2D Dubins problem and is expanded upon by considering a possible detour. The feasibility of the combined path is dependent on a specific ratio. The optimal path for scenarios where fuel consumption is a priority and when velocity and altitude are constrained are examined. The optimal air route for situations where taking the shortest route is a priority and when constraints related to control are factored in is also investigated.

The low-energy electronic structure of an unbiased bilayer graphene, characterized by quadratic dispersions at two Fermi points when high-order contributions are disregarded, differs qualitatively from that of single-layer graphene. We found that this difference leads to short-range interactions that are marginally relevant. Through the use of the renormalization group to investigate these interactions' effects on low-energy physics, it has been observed that, in both layers, two Fermi points will be qualitatively altered, developing a van Hove singularity that creates numerous instabilities towards ordering, including various broken symmetries such as layer-wise, spin-triplet, and spin-triplet+sublattice condensates. Moreover, it was determined that this model is susceptible to a continuous transition similar to that of the universal XY spin model, which may potentially be realized in the experiment.

The conformation of surface molecules greatly affects their functions. For Sc2TbN@C80, the conformation directly relates to the presence of an electric and a magnetic dipole moment. As a result, the adsorption of this molecule on a substrate changes the work function, with variations caused by the conformation-dependent electric dipole moment. Moreover, the magnetic properties of the conformation affect the exchange field, which is reflected in the adsorbed molecule's magnetization. To study these properties, the Confinement Quantum Chemistry method is employed on a WN@C80/( graphene/Ni(111) ) system to simulate Sc2TbN@C80. This model shows that at 300 K, the molecule exhibits a bent conformation with significantly enhanced work function and no magnetization. Conversely, the calculated results at 0 K indicate a linear conformation with a substantial exchange field and a corresponding magnetization. Notably, the work function significantly decreases upon conformational change from bent to linear. These simulations also predict that the molecule's conformation undergoes a phase transition at a specific thermal energy level between these two states, with the linear conformation becoming dynamically stable above this energy level.

The internet of things encompasses a network of interconnected devices, which includes various non-standard gadgets, traditionally unlinked to the internet, at an exponentially growing pace. Data security and user privacy concerns loom large over the IoT landscape, where devices operate on low power. Conventional encryption methods are unsuitable for these devices, necessitating a need for contemporary lightweight algorithms tailored for IoT settings, which this communication seeks to summarize.

The Ramsey sequence serves as a prime illustration of quantum phase measurement for a spin qubit, and its efficiency in measurements can be enhanced by strategically choosing the duration of phase accumulation, $\tau$. A sequential Bayesian experimental approach is employed to determine this duration in low-accuracy Ramsey measurements, and when repeated under the same conditions, it yields more accurate results than a traditional posterior-sampled approach. Furthermore, the adaptive methodology demonstrated here can be applied to other quantum measurement techniques, such as the standard Ramsey sequence, Jordan operator interferometry, and Zeno quench measurement.

Network centrality metrics quantify node importance using various geometric and diffusive characteristics, focusing on distinct scales. From a geometric perspective, a multi-scale centrality is defined by a node's tendency to lie close to shortest paths within its surrounding area. The Gromov centrality metric gauges importance at different network scales based on the size of the neighborhood and recovers well-known metrics as limiting cases. It is demonstrated that the Gromov centrality is highly computationally efficient to calculate due to its linear time complexity and dependent variables. The versatility and practical value of this multi-scale centrality method are illustrated through real-world network examples.

From a purely non-relativistic perspective, we derive the Poisson equation solution for empty space in a scenario with a rotating gravitational system, analogous to the Sun, and consider the implications of this solution for the behavior of test objects within its gravitational field. The general solution to the Poisson equation, expressed in terms of the distance r and angle θ, is shown to exhibit properties consistent with Newton's inverse square law of gravitation to the lowest order approximation. This analysis yields two notable outcomes when considered up to the second-order approximation: firstly, the apparent halving of rotational velocity, and secondly, the existence of an equilibrium position stable against small oscillations, in contrast to the conventional static model of gravitation. This study provides a foundational understanding of the gravitational behavior of test objects within a static and rotating gravitational system, serving as a preliminary step towards developing a comprehensive theory of gravitation capable of describing complex systems, including binary star systems, by employing Gauss's law for gravitational interaction.

Sets of matrix pencils sharing the same Kronecker canonical form are classified under strict equivalence into infinite groups called bundles. Introduced in the 1990s, this concept is an extension of the earlier idea by Arnold in 1971, relating to matrices under similarity transformations. Despite substantial research on the topology of bundles of matrix pencils, some key issues remain unresolved. Specifically, open questions include characterizing closure inclusions among bundles and determining whether these bundles are open within their own closures. This paper addresses these queries, revisiting existing notions and offering proof of the openness of bundles for matrices, as well as matrix polynomials within their respective closures.

The $C^*$-algebra formalism of topological T-duality developed by Mathai and Rosenberg is applied to a broad class of topological spaces encompassing torus bundles, nilmanifolds, and other examples from string theory. By constructing T-duals from commutative $C^*$-algebras with ${\mathbb R}^n$ action, we establish a simple method for achieving this transformation. Our work rigorously addresses almost abelian solvmanifolds across arbitrary dimensions, providing clear, comprehensive, and well-defined geometric constructs in comparison to existing literature.

Cohen-Addad, Filtser, Klein, and Le created a stochastic graph embedding method in their 2020 work, which enabled the preservation of short paths and allowed for a two-sided performance guarantee in terms of the original and resulting graph diameters. Their method involved first taking a probabilistic map of the input graph and then reducing it to one with bounded treewidth. Their research focused on investigating the feasibility of developing similar embedding techniques for more complex graphs, which do not have a fixed boundary. Their previous work showed that an embedding with a performance guarantee similar to minor-free graphs is achievable for small treewidth. Now, they investigated and confirmed the possibility of an embedding with similar performance guarantee for minor-free graphs with a bounded treewidth. Additionally, they developed an embedding method with a performance guarantee close to linear for boundedly treewidth graphs with n vertices. Furthermore, they established the intractability of determining if an embedding with a performance guarantee better than linear is achievable for all graphs with n vertices and treewidth at most w, for all w values greater than 5, based on a previously established intractability problem when treewidth is at least 4.

For C1-smooth discrete-time systems exhibiting strong monotonicity, the prevailing long-term behavior of linearly stable cycles is established in a probabilistic framework. This research then extends to periodic parabolic equations and reveals new findings regarding the ubiquity of periodic solution convergence. Notably, in a particular set of N-dimensional equations, the majority of initial conditions are aligned with a converging periodic solution.

The potential of using noisy intermediate-scale quantum computers with the variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) lies in molecular simulations, where accurately transforming coefficients is crucial but complicated by measurement errors in qubits. Current research has focused on optimizing circuit depths rather than reducing the importance of lower-weight coefficients. Our approach, the qubit-excitation-based adaptive VQE (QABE-VQE), addresses this by applying a systematic framework for extracting coefficients from a chosen variational circuit. By minimizing the impact of noisy qubits on coefficient transformations, we achieved significant improvements in convergence rates. Additionally, we applied our QABE-VQE method in ab initio calculations of small molecules and hydrogen chains with increased qubit errors, where it substantially enhanced the algorithm's tolerance to noise. Our findings indicate that by reducing low-weight coefficient variance, we can achieve a more stable and accurate VQE model, where both the circuit depth and model stability are improved.

A key characteristic of deep generative models is the complex interplay between representation, its distribution, and the way it is mapped to data, an interrelationship that poses difficulties for understanding and optimizing these models. This work proposes a framework for studying these models by assuming a standard posterior distribution for the intermediate steps of a decoding process. This approach has two main benefits. Firstly, it provides an interpretative model, placing the Bayesian neural network framework within a broader context of linear Gaussian models. Secondly, it offers a concise method for estimating parameters in models such as variational autoencoders, minimizing both training and inference times. Our approach also has a range of practical applications, including the capacity to perform Bayesian inference, transfer knowledge across similar datasets, balance between different decoding steps, and determine the optimal decoding steps for tasks such as compression and image creation.

The discovery of a common-spectrum process in recent NANOGrav findings has led to theories suggesting it could be linked to primordial magnetic fields, which would generate a high-frequency gravitational wave background.  We explore how this background might affect cosmological precision, focusing on its potential impact on the Hubble tension resolution.  If the stochastic gravitational wave background is strong enough to resonate with the primordial magnetic fields' characteristic scale, it could amplify the gravitational waves by a factor.  Within certain parameters, the amplified gravitational waves could ease the Hubble tension, yet persist at frequencies detectable by future laser interferometers.  Leveraging numerical simulations and analytical approximations, we mapped out possible inflationary scenarios supporting both a gravitational wave background detectable by future detectors and a significant reduction of the Hubble tension.  We found that a laser interferometer with enough sensitivity to detect the stochastic gravitational wave background generated by primordial magnetic fields would also be capable of constraining these fields' properties.

Our study presents the first survey of molecular emissions from a great comet,
conducted using the ALMA Atacama Compact Array. We identified CS J = 1-0,
CS J = 2-1, and C2H+ J = 1-0 emissions originating from the coma of Comet C/2015
ER61; other molecules such as HCN, CH3CN, and HNC were also detected as well as the J = 1-0 emissions of water and ammonia. We analyzed the variability of emission lines over six observations to understand the spout-like source of CS, located 5.5 to 6.5 kilometers from the comet's center. Our co-rotation model suggests this source is either co-rotating with the rest of the comet or located behind it. We developed a new technique to combine the Alfvén wave model and a hydrodynamics model to analyze CS and C2H+ emissions, revealing that their origins likely extend beyond the comet's photosphere. Our analysis also suggests that CN and CH3CN emissions are not from the jet but instead originate from the water group. Additionally, we observed two distinct water gas clouds, one located 5-6 kilometers from the comet's center and another much larger one (~ 500 kilometers in diameter), the more extensive water cloud is most likely related to the water rich mixture of the comet. Our observations of Comet C/2015 ER61 provide the first direct evidence that CS

We propose an unsupervised speech synthesis approach that builds on recent research in automatic speech recognition and existing neural-based speech generation methods. Employing only raw, unlabeled audio and text data, as well as a dictionary, our technique enables high-quality speech synthesis without requiring a prelabeled dataset. Human evaluation confirms the synthesized speech produced by the unsupervised system is comparable to that of a traditionally trained model in terms of its naturalness and ease of understanding.

This research employs the Tsallis holographic dark energy model in two scenarios, 
non-interacting and interacting, to calculate essential parameters for the energy 
density equation of state within the FRW universe, analogous to a quintessence model.
We will reassess complex quintessence by modifying its potential and analyzing 
scalar field dynamics, followed by examining the differences in and stability 
of two scenarios, namely non-interacting and interacting.
We will examine the interaction between this type of dark energy and another form 
of dark energy using the fitted $\Omega_{Q}(z)$ estimate.
We will then investigate the stability of two types of dark energy solutions, 
namely non-interacting and interacting, by modifying the energy density equation of 
state to account for the influence of parameters on the stability of these 
solutions, illustrating how interactions impact the stability of these solutions.

Multi-objective mixed-integer non-linear programming problems frequently arise in real-world contexts, notably in mechanical engineering. A novel approach, combining multi-criteria branch-and-bound and non-dominated sorting genetic algorithm 2, is proposed for approximating Pareto fronts for such problems. A computational study, comparing this proposed hybrid method to non-dominated sorting genetic algorithm 2, demonstrates its efficacy with real-world and test cases. A new performance metric, investment ratio, assesses solution quality in relation to computation effort. Results from evaluating this proposed algorithm on five mechanical engineering and two mathematical test cases indicate its competitiveness for solving MO-MINLPs.

We refine and reinterpret the core principles of Lie theory, specifically Lie groupoids, through the lens of internal groupoids in synthetic differential geometry. Key concepts are re-expressed, including path sources and integrated $A$-paths. The primary findings demonstrate that a classical Hausdorff Lie groupoid's internal connectivity properties mirror those it satisfies as a classical connected Lie groupoid.

The Dynaswap project is focused on developing a robust, trustworthy architecture for safeguarding electronic health records and genomic data processing. This goal revolves around safeguarding this sensitive data as it is shared for research purposes. In order to achieve this, Dynaswap integrates cutting-edge software security methods, as well as the use of community-based standards and protocols, to facilitate widespread adoption. This paper outlines the projected infrastructure and user experience for Dynaswap, incorporating prototype development, functionality explanations, and assessments based on existing data sharing projects. Prototypes have been built for both the initial data collection phase and the long-term data storage period, emphasizing the utilization of widely accepted common standards and procedures. Dynaswap's future plans include the continuation of prototype refinement and widespread deployment, which would encompass secure computing environments, network connections to multiple data storage facilities, and a user-friendly interface for data submission. This infrastructure will provide users with a comprehensive understanding of data sharing regulations, as well as comprehensive support. Prototypes have demonstrated that Dynaswap can effectively integrate software security methods to support secure computing environments, as well as the utilization of common standards and procedures for data processing. This has also shown that Dynaswap's long-term data storage approach compares favorably to that of the National Institutes of Health's BioSample Database. Dynaswap's user-friendly architecture and interfaces have also demonstrated the capacity to educate users on data sharing regulations and provide comprehensive support. This includes the initial data collection phase and the long-term data storage period

Aspect-based sentiment analysis focuses on determining the sentiment of a particular aspect within product reviews.  Most approaches frame sentiment prediction as a supervised classification task, overlooking the fact that sentences often naturally convey opinions.  Additionally, many studies rely on explicitly labeled sentiment orientations, neglecting the potential for extracting sentiment implicitly from text.  This paper investigates the application of pre-trained models on unsupervised data through contrastive learning to capture implicit sentiment.  We further enhance this pre-trained model using a variety of enhanced supervised pre-training tasks that incorporate sampling techniques from real-world data.  Our results on six datasets demonstrate the superiority of our proposed method over existing approaches by accurately identifying implicit sentiment from a broader range of sentiment orientations.

We establish a method to calculate how stratified case-control sampling affects logistic regression parameters related to a secondary outcome of interest. This is particularly significant when conducting mediation analysis with binary outcome and mediator variables in case-control studies. Our results facilitate estimation using M-estimation techniques and the maximum likelihood method. A simulation study validates the and demonstrates the applicability of our findings.

This research delves into secure communication systems for multiple users that utilize reconfigurable intelligent surfaces to compensate for hardware limitations.
We simultaneously adjust the base station's beamforming vectors and the phase shifts on the RIS to achieve the highest possible weighted minimum secrecy rate under constraints for the base station's power output and RIS element limitations.
To address this optimization challenge, we split the problem into two simpler subproblems and use the block coordinate descent approach to iteratively solve for these subproblems through different optimization algorithms.
Numerical simulations confirm that our proposed method offers superior performance advantages over existing secure communication systems, particularly in scenarios with varying levels of hardware impairments.

We begin by defining a task for few-shot continual learning and propose a theory to explain how executive function works through a self-updating decision-making system that reprocesses perception data through a review of past experiences in order to minimize prediction errors. This idea becomes practical due to the incorporation of a memory mechanism and a pre-trained neural network that is predisposed to follow rules of effective learning and adapts to optimize its chances of long-term success. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our model of executive function can facilitate the development of hypothesis testing as an internal reasoning process and might provide insight into observed abilities of human learning and the organization of the human brain.

We studied the solar wind energy flux near the center of our solar system using data from four different close approaches to the sun with the Parker Solar Probe. We categorized the data into periods when it was observing the "north" polar region of a solar magnetic field and when it was observing the "south" polar region. We found significant differences in solar wind energy by looking at specific intervals: 11-month averages of data from the solar wind's velocity distribution, its pressure over distance, and its overall energy transmission. These findings showed that the most significant variations occurred in the solar wind's velocity, its pressure over distance, and its overall energy transmission during the different polar region observations. Furthermore, we calculated an average energy flux of 6.58 x 10^6 W/m^2/steradian for both the "north" and "south" polar regions, which is comparable to 4-box model predictions. However, we discovered that the solar wind energy is being transmitted more efficiently at the lower frequencies during closer approaches to the sun, but not at higher frequencies. By comparing different periods of solar activity, we found that the solar wind energy is higher near the equator during more active periods, which is reflected in the increased velocity and its correlation with lower density and faster velocity in different directions.

In an updated version of our previous work, we establish a connection between how a group influences a algebraic structure and a specific type of complex geometric mapping. By establishing this link, we demonstrate that certain complex geometric mappings result from a group's effect on an algebraic structure. Additionally, we identify the conditions under which these mappings exhibit key characteristics.

We show that any family of maximal almost-disjoint sets can be eliminated via a specific method of adding new elements that preserves the cardinality of $P$-points. Using this finding, we establish that it is possible in a specific set of circumstances that the first uncountable ordinal is less than the least cardinality for uniformization, but the least cardinality for amalgamation is greater, resolving two problems that have been outstanding for nearly 20 years and a further issue proposed by Brendle. Furthermore, we will provide a simplified explanation for why it is consistent that $\mathfrak{u}<\mathfrak{s}$ as proven by Blass and Shelah.

The introduction of $q$-deformation into optomechanical systems reveals opportunities to amplify non-traditional optical phenomena. This insight drives an investigation of the optical behavior within a linearly coupled $q$-deformed optomechanical system. Composed of two deformed cavities interacting with mechanical mirrors and coupled through a transmission parameter, this study reveals that $q$-deformation enhances the speed and magnitude of phase transitions and optical band gaps. Moreover, for a specific range of $q$ values, the model exhibits symmetry in optical behavior, including optomechanical resonance and band gap formation. Additionally, theoretical analysis demonstrates the theoretical minimum time required for optomechanical coupling to achieve coherency. This is similar in magnitude to the time required for classical mechanical coupling to induce a classical transition.

In a previous study, I developed a model where the Two-Rotors Model's negative scissors states, consisting of two-sided classical bodies, exhibited 1 |K| = 1; 0 components and negative space parity. Building on this work, I explored reflections in a plane that aligns with the rotors' symmetry axes, resulting in R-negative states with positive parity. Furthermore, I established a connection between reflections and R-operations, relating them to specific internal changes within the rotors, which I then used to calculate and compare the electromagnetic transition strengths of these states with those of their positive scissors mode counterparts.

A new method inspired by finite volume schemes leverages neural networks to solve partial differential equations. By utilizing the cell-average representation of the solution, the method accommodates a broad range of conservation laws while avoiding the resolution of shocks. This approach simplifies the challenge of accurately modelling stiff source or flux terms. Furthermore, the method can easily be adapted for multi-dimensional problems and the semi-discrete neural network scheme can be transformed into a fully discrete solution using a Runge-Kutta method.

The ALICE Collaboration has finalized the upgrade of its detector, with the current phase involving testing to mark the beginning of data collection for LHC Run 3. In conjunction, studies on the experiment's future are underway, with the primary goal being to establish the ALICE Collaboration's objectives for LHC Run 3 and beyond. In the upcoming decades, the experiment is poised to play a pivotal role in the research into QCD and the early universe, with the findings expected to be published in numerous analyses spanning multiple detectors. This article summarizes the experiment's upgrades and the results, as well as delving into the prospects for LHC Run 3 and beyond.

The Unruh effect can emerge not only in the traditional intratime domain but also in the timelike domain of a specific spacetime, specifically around the light cone's timelike portion in one-dimensional motion, where the stress tensor's vacuum expectation value exhibits a nonzero force. We investigated this intratime and timelike Unruh effect by analyzing two quantum field theories developing in opposite directions. One theory starts from the past's light cone, while the other extends to the future's light cone. By examining the mutual entanglement between these two theories, particularly the geometric phase associated with this entanglement, we discovered that it mirrors the intratime Unruh effect and can serve as an indicator for the timelike Unruh effect.

One of the primary objectives of Information Extraction involves recognizing event descriptions along with the entities involved, allowing for the accumulation of quantitative information which can be employed in various applications such as forecasting, surveillance, and societal analysis. This information can have a significant impact in areas like economics, politics, and medicine. While several datasets for Event Extraction have been developed, the available options are limited when working with languages other than English. This paper presents a new multilingual event extraction dataset without relying on annotated data. MEE, the proposed dataset, includes descriptions of events in eight distinct languages and includes over 13,000 manually annotated event categories. These entities are also accompanied by a detailed temporal framework representing their relationship. To our knowledge, the proposed dataset is the largest comprehensive event extraction collection available in eight languages to date. Experiments conducted using transfer learning techniques demonstrate the effectiveness of current state-of-the-art models, including BERT and ALBERT, in extracting events from multiple languages when trained on the collection. However, the results indicate room for further improvement in multilingual event extraction.

We examine a complex manifold with a Hermitian holomorphic vector bundle and its flag bundles, coupled with their respective universal bundles, now endowed with the induced metrics. A crucial aspect of our research involves establishing the validity, pointwise in Chern forms, of the universal push-forward formula for all universal bundles. A fundamental step toward our proof is explicitly determining, at each point of the flag bundle, the Chern curvature of the universal bundles, as endowed with their induced metrics. This leads to the development of an alternative approach to the Jacobi-Trudi identity using differential forms, as well as confirmation of the positivity of specific Chern forms for Griffiths semipositive vector bundles, thus partially supporting Griffiths' conjecture on characteristic forms of positive characteristic.

Observations from the XMM-Newton telescope revealed how a clumpy stellar wind from a companion star in high mass X-ray binaries impacts the variable absorption and timing properties of the emitted X-rays. We analyzed a 7.22 day dataset from Cyg X-1 in its hard state and discovered notable changes in its X-ray spectrum and corona properties when the wind density increased. The wind's density varies with the Star's orbital period due to its interaction with the outermost binary orbit. The increased density leads to a harder X-ray spectrum, reduced fluorescence radius, and a longer lag in the X-ray variations. The variations in Cyg X-1 differ from those expected in an environment with a constant wind due to its dynamic behavior.

The Yang-Mills-aether theory is analyzed to understand the implications of introducing non-abelian aether-like terms that violate Lorentz symmetry, specifically within thermal quantum field theory. By incorporating temperature effects and spatial compactification via Thermofield Dynamics, corrections to the non-abelian Stefan-Boltzmann law and non-abelian Casimir energy and pressure are calculated for both zero and finite temperatures.

Researchers have long sought to bridge the gap between syntax and semantics parsing but so far have had to make a choice between excelling in one area at the cost of the other, contradicting research highlighting the complex interactions between the two. To address this issue, we examine multiple model designs capable of tapping into rich data in the Universal Decompositional Semantics (UDS) dataset, parsing it alongside Universal Dependencies for high-performance results in both formats. Analyzing the effects of combining syntax and semantics parsing reveals patterns that are supported by linguistic theory at their interface. Moreover, we examine the effectiveness of joint modeling in multiple languages, discovering analogous trends in 8 languages tested.

The formation of magnetically-driven jets from a spinning black hole following a compact binary merger is a potential explanation for the actrion S and the GW190521 event. These jets can create kilonova ejecta that power an unusual optical and gravitational wave emission, known as a tidal disruption event. Previous studies of merger simulations have identified another possible mechanism for driving these outflows - the unleashed neutrino-flux radiating from the accretion disk. In our research, we have modeled how this energy drives an outflow from a disk that's cooling quickly, either directly taking energy from the disk or through jet formation. We found that the outflow is influenced by both mechanisms, with the outflow rate reaching approximately 0.1 solar masses per second. However, the energy carried by the outflow in both scenarios is similar and capable of explaining the observed emission in the GW190521 event, an effect also producible by magnetically-driven jets.

We undertook a statistical investigation into tidal features surrounding early-type galaxies of massive proportions, utilizing data from the Hyper Suprime-Cam Subaru Strategic Program. Our analysis revealed that approximately 8.6% of 264,421 galaxies, selected through volume-limiting criteria, possessed distinct tidal features, with a ratio of light from the features to the central galaxy exceeding a certain threshold. Confining our focus to galaxies of mass above 10^11 M_sun and within a redshift range of 0.05-0.20, we discovered the frequency of tidal structures in these galaxies to be around 5.8%. Our observations indicated that galaxies experiencing a significant loss of material due to interactions with other galaxies had a higher mass, on average, compared to non-interacting galaxies. Additionally, we determined the frequency of tidal features in galaxies of mass ranging from one billion to one and a half billion solar masses to be between 4.2% and 5.4%. Our best estimate for the frequency of tidal features in galaxies of mass above one billion solar masses is around 5.4%. Our analysis also revealed that galaxies exhibiting robust tidal features tended to have slower rotation curves compared to galaxies without such features. Our findings may imply that galaxies of massive proportions interact with other galaxies relatively infrequently and that tidal features observed in these galaxies could be remnants from mergers occurring approximately one billion years ago.

This paper is a component of a research series focusing on the Azimuthally Symmetric Theory of Gravitation (ASTG), a theoretical framework derived from the established equation by Laplace and Poisson. Our findings indicate that, under specific conditions dependent on the object's spin, the ASTG can generate repulsive gravitational fields in the polar regions of massive objects, thereby shedding new light on the phenomenon of outflows as a manifestation of repulsive gravity. This process is an integral component of star formation and has been the subject of extensive debate regarding its origins. This paper diverges from the conventional understanding of gravitation, presenting it as a force that, in certain contexts, drives material apart rather than pulling it together towards a central point. Furthermore, we present empirical evidence that suggests the Azimuthally Symmetric Gravitational Field derived from the ASTG can effectively resolve a theoretical dilemma surrounding massive star formation known as the Radiation Problem, where the high levels of radiation from the developing star can prevent further accretion of matter. Our analysis reveals that, contrary to expectations, accretion continues even past the estimated threshold of about 8-10 times the mass of our sun, as the gravitational force exerted by the equatorial plane enables in-falling material to accelerate towards the developing star. In contrast, the ASTG-generated repulsive gravitational field in the polar regions significantly impedes gas flow towards the star and is likely to either block or divert outbursts from the star's polar regions

We have obtained a first, we can say multi-epoch, survey of optical radiation from a significant sample of Fast Radio Bursts at very high cadence. Our extensive observations of 22 FRBs were carried out with a high sensitivity and covered a significant range of distances from the FRBs' sources, measured in millions of light years. Despite our study with considerable light year depth, we did not see any optical radiation from the FRBs that can be used for determining the redshifts of their sources. Our measurement also showed that, on average, the brightness of the optical radiation from the FRBs' sources is very small. Moreover, we did not see any recurrence in our FRBs' sample that can be used for determining the redshifts of their sources. Our measurement and findings have the capability of being extended to all the FRBs' observation methods including wide-field, wide-depth and deep surveys including those with VLT, it has any.

The combination of chirped pulse amplification and nonlinear optical systems has been the foundation for significant progress in numerous sectors, including semiconductors, communications, biology, defense, and national security. However, accurately modeling these laser systems using CPA and NLO is a complex task due to their interconnected linear and nonlinear processes, and the high variability in available modeling frameworks. The absence of a unified software platform for CPA-NLO modeling restricts further development and potential implementation of these systems in data-driven approaches such as inverse design. We introduce a modular software model that encompasses various amplifier configurations and nonlinear techniques to provide time and frequency-resolved electromagnetic field data and essential physical properties, enabling characteristics of energy, fluence, and spectral distribution. To showcase its capabilities, we apply our software to the LCLS-II photo-injector laser, an example of a complex CPA-NLO system requiring high power and precise control.

Multimodal language generation capabilities of models like GPT-2 and GPT-3 can be
utilized for producing high-quality text with specific visual attributes. To integrate
visual elements in text generation, we propose a novel approach that incorporates
image features into text prediction. Specifically, we identified three challenges in
visual-driven text generation: pinning, image replication, and diverse image-based
text generation. To address these issues, we developed three novel architectures:
Visual Embedding Pinning, Replication Distillation, and Diversity Promoted Generation
all leveraging VGG-19's image feature extraction. Experimental results demonstrate that
these models effectively produce text with accurate visual attributes in multiple
sentences.

We introduce an upgraded RingCT protocol that supports stealth addresses in conjunction with Delegated Proof of Stake, resulting in Delegated RingCT.
The Delegated RingCT scheme is comprised of an integrated signature and encryption framework, combining a public key encryption protocol and two types of signatures along with linkable ring signatures, alongside non-interactive zero-knowledge proofs.
A comprehensive description of Delegated RingCT, along with security evidence and an implemented prototype, are presented, which we subsequently test through benchmarking analysis.
While Delegated RingCT may not possess the same level of anonymity compared to other RingCT variations, we propose that its ability to be compatible with DPoS consensus mechanisms provides a reasonable trade-off for enabling a more efficient and scalable decentralised cryptocurrency with preserved anonymity capabilities.

In 2015, CERN introduced "Emittance Scans," a new fast luminosity separation scanning method at the Large Hadron Collider. These scans were consistently carried out during physics production runs, utilizing full-intensity beams at the CMS experiment's interaction point. The emittance scans allowed for the simultaneous measurement of beam properties and closed orbits at the level of individual bunches, yielding a detailed understanding of long-range beta functions and machine performance. The capability to access extensive beam data offline enabled comprehensive beam diagnostics, including the recovery of functioning beam monitors and improvement of beam delivery efficiency. The emittance scans also provided an effective technique for demonstrating the accurate formation of compact beams at the CMS interaction point, thereby confirming the accuracy of simulated beam models.

Recent breakthroughs in artificial neural networks have accelerated the growth of data-driven modeling in mechanics, making cooperative modeling more feasible than ever before. The traditional approach to modeling in mechanics involves isolating a distinct problem for systematic analysis, due to the vast variety of scenarios present in nature and materials. However, many phenomena exhibit subtle variations that cannot be fully captured through prior knowledge alone. This necessitates the use of data-driven modeling, which strives to complement traditional modeling by identifying the uncharted aspects of phenomena through experimental or sensory inputs. Historically, data-driven modeling has been a one-way process where preconized models are adjusted to fit experimental data, resulting in little cooperation between theoretical and experimental perspectives. This article, however, describes a novel cooperative data-driven modeling approach utilizing machine learning, where theoretical preconceptions adjust the data and experimental perspectives synchronize the interpretation of inputs. The article provides an overview of recent advancements in machine learning, particularly focusing on unsupervised learning using variational auto-encoders and its applications in cooperative modeling. It also discusses the challenges and promising avenues for further research in cooperative data-driven modeling.

This research examines the decay of the $\Upsilon(10753)$ into a $\Upsilon(nS)$
state accompanied by $\pi^+\pi^-$ particles, where $n=1,2,3$. It's assumed
$\Upsilon(10753)$ belongs to a typical bottomonium under the $4S$-$3D$ mixing
scenario. We find that these specific decay processes have relatively large
branching ratios of $10^{-4}$ to $10^{-3}$ and, notably, align with Belle's
experimental findings, validating our previous assignment of the $\Upsilon(10753)$
bottomonium to the $4S$-$3D$ mixing scheme. Further validation of this work
could be achieved through testing with Belle II experiment data.

This paper presents a novel optimization technique called AskewSGD to efficiently train deep neural networks with quantized weights. Initially, we transform the quantized neural network training into a constrained optimization problem that can be refined by iteratively relaxing its constraints. Our method, AskewSGD, is based on Newton's strategy with perturbed interval constraints that prevent the network's weights from exceeding defined integer bounds. AskewSGD performs exceptionally well with symmetric and asymmetric quantization schemes across various number of bits (2 to 64). It effectively handles weight scaling issues associated with asymmetric quantization by adjusting the optimization process. Our method generalizes the current state-of-the-art approaches and offers improved initial solutions for standard datasets such as ResNet34 and VGG16 on CIFAR10 using quantized weights. AskewSGD's performance is further enhanced by its adaptability to vary the number of bits for different layers in a neural network. Our empirical analysis demonstrates that AskewSGD's efficiency stems from its ability to converge towards optimal solutions by converging toward stationary points of the reformulated optimization problem on a local scale.

The Continuum Soft Robot project utilizes fully flexible mechanical systems to achieve robots that more closely resemble the anatomy of invertebrate creatures and flexible body parts of vertebrates. To introduce the concepts and challenges of this innovative area in robotics, we will be adopting a control theorist's approach, simplifying the entry into this field by systematically presenting current research and future obstacles through a uniform language and organized structure. The primary hurdles to participating in this area lie in understanding the inherent characteristics of continuum robots and their accompanying difficulties, followed by recognizing the importance of modeling in addressing these challenges. We will begin by defining continuum robots and their distinctive attributes, before providing a comprehensive model-based control framework to synthesize controllers for these robots. Finally, we will detail the model-based control methods currently in use and their respective limitations, followed by presenting the inherent obstacles that must be overcome in this field and proposing potential solutions.

The Jacobi group $G^J_1(\mathbb{R})$ - specifically its semi-direct product of ${\rm SL}(2,\mathbb{R})$ with $H_1$ - can be embedded into a realisation of ${\rm Sp}(2,\mathbb{R})$ via a 4x4 matrix representation. One-forms and orthogonal dual vector fields are then computed in the S-coordinates for $G^J_1(\mathbb{R})$ to find a metric depending on parameters $(\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\delta)$. Additionally, metrics on ${\rm SL}(2,\mathbb{R})$ depending on $(\alpha,\beta)$, and in the Siegel-Jacobi upper half-plane, $\mathcal{X}^J_1$, are described in the known balanced Kähler metric depending on $(\alpha,\gamma)$. Left-invariant metrics on the manifolds $\mathcal{X}_1\times\mathbb{R}^3$ depending on parameters $(\alpha,\gamma,\delta)$, specifically on $\tilde{\mathcal{B}}_{\gamma,\delta}$ and on $\tilde{\mathcal{J}}_{\alpha,\delta}$, are determined in the left-invariant metric depending on $(\alpha,\beta)$, and the right-action $\Delta$ on $\mathcal{X}^J_1$

Verifying facts using structured data can be difficult, necessitating a model's
understanding of both language and symbolic computations involving data in
tables. Despite pre-trained language models excelling in confirming simple
assertions, they often falter when handling complex assertions requiring
multiple calculations. In our research, we alleviate this challenge by breaking
down intricate assertions into manageable sub-problems. By employing the
synthesized programs from a weakly-supervised parser, we suggest an innovative
method for generating a simulated dataset that assists in the training of our
decomposition-based fact verification model. Our proposed method relies on the
resolution of these simplified problems within the synthesized programs to
confirm the factual statements. Through experiments conducted on two popular
datasets – WikiTableQuestions and WikiJump – we demonstrate that our model's
training on this artificially created dataset results in consistently superior
performance when compared to other leading techniques.

The state of the art in learned synthetic image generation involves generative adversarial networks. Initial breakthroughs in the field relied on unsupervised approaches, however, current advancements are primarily based on labelled data, leading to increased control and flexibility in the resulting models. A key challenge in the area of supervised GANs is developing an efficient unsupervised method for organizing the generated images. This paper presents a novel approach that utilizes an auxiliary latent space to condition these networks in a supplementary manner. This conditionality is applied at both the data and test stages, leveraging the understanding gained from an additional dataset, but only in an unsupervised capacity, as with identity conditions and scene graphs. The proposed method provides an efficient and flexible visual representation of generated images, while its auxiliary approach allows for the creation of multiple creative visions, unlike traditional conditioning techniques which typically leave little to the imagination. The research further explores the diversity of conditions, achieving a comprehensive set of creative visions in the resulting models.

To perform Bayesian inference using nested sampling, a specific prior sampling approach must be used, which requires exploring the high-dimensional parameter space efficiently to compile a representative list of samples from regions with higher posterior probabilities. Researchers have developed methods like Markov Chain Monte Carlo and kernel-based techniques to tackle this process, which often involve complex algorithms to guide sampling. In contrast, alternative approaches like kernel nested sampling rely on non-Markovian techniques to achieve similar results. A new study aims to develop an efficient sampling method using steps from the posterior distribution, which can be decoupled and calculated multiple times. We demonstrate that this approach, dubbed Step SAMPLer, offers significant improvements in efficiency compared to traditional nested sampling methods. Furthermore, we show that implementing Step SAMPLer within kernels, which are inherently non-Markovian, can accelerate nested sampling by an order of magnitude or more in many cases. We illustrate the effectiveness of Step SAMPLer through numerical examples and compare it with other cutting-edge sampling methods. Moreover, we shed new light on the theoretical limitations of all nested sampling algorithms, which have previously remained unaddressed in the literature.

In fault-tolerant distance labelling, we're tasked with assigning brief descriptions to the points in a network so that knowing any three points' labels allows us to deduce the direct distance between any two of them, excluding the third. Our work proves that any weighted network with a specific layout (or in fact any network with limited separating elements) allows the assignment of brief descriptions with a specific length that covers the network in such a way that it remains accurate even after the removal of any single element. Additionally, we propose a method for quickly and efficiently designing such descriptions, which works within a specific time limit for networks with specific types of weights and network layouts.

In this theoretical study, we explore two-particle correlations in time and frequency for a Bose-Hubbard model subject to external driving and dissipation, specifically at and around a point where energy is resonant. We find through numerical simulations that dissipation causes a distinct low-frequency pattern to emerge in frequency-based correlations when the system is in a superfluid state, whereas noise remains high in a normal phase under the same conditions. When the system is in a superfluid state, fluctuations in time-based correlations follow a specific, non-regular pattern that is inversely related to the rate of dissipation, whereas in a normal state, fluctuations are uniformly high. These findings offer a clear indicator of dissipation and suggest a possible experimental approach for observing superfluid states in systems subject to external driving and dissipation.

For a given second-order linear elliptic equation with coefficients $A$, $\mathbf{b}$ and a parameter $\epsilon$, defined within a bounded $\mathbb{R}^2$ domain $\Omega$, with $\mathbf{b}$ in $L^2_{\text{loc}}(\Omega; \mathbb{R}^2)$ and $A$ a symmetric, uniformly elliptic matrix in $L^{\infty}(\Omega;\mathbb{R}^{2\times 2})$, we obtain a unique $W^{1,p}_\text{loc}(\Omega;\mathbb{R}^N)$ weak solution, with $2 \le p < \infty$, for which neither the Jacobian nor the divergence of $\mathbf{b}$ lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb{R}^N)$.

To ensure that medical imaging models produce accurate predictions, it is crucial to implement out-of-distribution detection capabilities. There are concerns that deep neural network-based detectors may not be reliable in this context, particularly given their inherent uncertainty. In an effort to improve out-of-distribution detection performance, this paper explores the integration of Gaussian Processes, due to their proven ability to accurately identify data anomalies. A Gaussian Processes layer is developed and incorporated into existing classification models, replacing traditional deep learning layers. Furthermore, a novel Gaussian Processes layer is combined with an uncertainty-based detection mechanism to produce a comprehensive out-of-distribution detection system. Experimental findings on a large medical dataset indicate that the proposed Gaussian Processes models demonstrate superior performance compared to existing approaches.

Quantum systems driven periodically exhibit unique dynamics, with the potential to explore previously uncharacterized phenomena. A prominent feature of these systems is the emergence of "quantum scars," which persist even in the infinite-time limit even for 3D systems. The article investigates the effects of periodically driving a 1D quantum system, where the interaction with a bath leads to thermalization among the eigenstates within a specific, narrowed-down subspace. Through the simulation of a cold atoms system subjected to a strong, periodic laser and in contact with a thermal bath, it is demonstrated that the system can achieve a rare, weakly-interacting Bose-Einstein condensation, specifically involving "scar-related" excitations, which are largely protected from dissipation by the quantum scar phenomenon. The article presents a theoretical approach to increase the "scarsity" of the system, thus allowing for the observation of Bose-Einstein condensation with high precision. This approach involves the removal of excitations at higher energy levels through incoherent dissipation, thereby increasing the condensate fraction within the system. The proposed method has the potential to be successfully implemented using current optical-trap technology, which is highly adaptable and expandable to more complex systems and scenarios.

The article establishes a gradual increase in the H\"older continuity of solutions to the Monge--Amp\`ere equation, with a bounded right-hand side, as the norm of the right-hand side increases. Specifically, if the right-hand side belongs to a $\beta$-H\"older continuous function, the solution will be uniformly $\beta$-H\"older continuous. Conversely, it's proven that if the right-hand side is Holder continuous at a single point, the solution will be locally H\"older continuous at that point, with the same exponent. This counteracts an example presented by J.J. Kornfeld and S. Orench in 1994, where a solution to the Monge--Amp\`ere equation is constructed with a right-hand side that is Holder continuous at a single point yet fails to be locally H\"older continuous everywhere.

Counting the recurrence of periodic events allows us to measure time. Historically, developing stable and accurate timekeeping devices was a significant undertaking. We will instead examine a different class of timekeeping devices, based on random clicking mechanisms. A comprehensive statistical analysis framework is developed to evaluate the effectiveness of these devices, with a specific example being a single two-level atom driven coherently and monitored via photodetection, representing a non-periodic optical clock. Using quantum jump simulations and the mesoscopic photon number distribution, our model reproduces the known master equation dynamics while offering additional insights. The statistical framework identifies suitable timekeepers by calculating correlation coefficients and the characteristic time scale of the Pearson correlation function. The results show that the time scale is directly proportional to the system's lifetime, the average photon number, and inversely proportional to the Rabi frequency.

This research centers on Software Defined Networks (SDN) to address the challenges of traffic engineering, fault prevention, and service delivery within reliability and energy constraints. To achieve these goals, we integrated open-flow based control planes with cloud-based distributed forwarding planes to support Fog-based SDN. Our model, F-SDF, incorporates three main components: effective service delivery through Fog-assisted topological mapping and traffic routing; fault detection and response by leveraging resource reallocation and service delivery optimization; and fault prevention by promoting network stability and redundancy. Our method, F-SDF, employs a two-stage approach, including real-time scheduling and online program optimization, which results in significant energy savings and delivery reliability enhancements. Our model's feasibility is demonstrated through simulations, which show a 60% decrease in reconfiguration frequency and a 40% reduction in energy consumption compared to current SDN methods.

Metric learning's pair-wise loss technique is centered around optimizing an embedding that maximizes similarity between images within the same class, minimizing distance between images in distinct classes. Various forms of pair-wise loss strategies have been proposed. To consolidate this diverse set of loss functions, we've isolated specific aspects that dictate how these functions manipulate the positioning of feature pairs. Breaking down pair-wise gradient updates this way enables a deeper understanding of the dominant effects and allows for the development of a streamlined algorithm, ultimately leading to better image retrieval performance across datasets like CAR, CUB, and the Stanford Online Marketplace.

In this context, we explore certain classes of holographic tensor networks, which can efficiently simulate various systems using the principle of minimization, serve as quantum codes to prevent information loss, and accurately describe phenomena exhibiting power-law behaviors. A key finding reveals that networks comprising a single type of tensor and possessing erasure correction capabilities can't simultaneously possess certain desirable traits - those that facilitate the efficient calculation of physical properties through an efficient tree structure and those necessary for the accurate description of power-law behaviors. This contradiction motivates the creation of network guidelines that utilize diverse types of tensors, allowing these networks to successfully capture the characteristics of systems exhibiting power-law behaviors while providing an efficient tree structure for calculating physical properties through simplification. A crucial assessment of these networks has further established their theoretical limits in successfully capturing the properties of systems undergoing phase transitions while efficiently representing various correlated phenomena.

Our study of magnetized radio filaments at the center of the galaxy utilizes Meerts et al's sample from the center of the galaxy. By looking at a filament's proximity to other filaments, we investigate if there are significant patterns in how closely they are related. However, since population statistics are being studied, the population is compared to randomly selected, straight-lined, and uniform filaments. By matching populations based on distance from the center, we find no substantial variation in the distance between filaments. Both populations average 0.35 degress and show identical distribution patterns with most distances being less than 0.6 degress. Furthermore, multiple filaments can form when there is a split or division of a single filament, evidenced by two close filaments being less than 0.1 degress apart and one more filament being at least 0.6 degress away. Additionally, we observe that parallel filaments can form branches, but not in population average.

A proposed paper suggests a new method of distributed leader-follower control for achieving conservation voltage reduction in unbalanced three-phase distribution systems by optimizing DERs through the scheduling of smart inverters. The method considers primary-secondary networks and loads influenced by voltage. The system complexity is minimized through the creation of zones in the network based on connectivity. To address non-linearities from load models and power flow, the paper suggests a linear approximation technique using Taylor expansion. The complexity of communication is also reduced through the creation of smaller groups within the network. The method's efficacy is demonstrated through simulation on a real U.S. medium-scale feeder, showing a performance comparable to a centralized approach and an ability to adapt to dynamic changes in the network.

We investigate non-stochastic bandits and experts in a delayed context, where delays are contingent upon specific arms. We aim to achieve the best possible regret analysis while also considering how to preempt delays to minimize total waiting time, even when hindsight is unavailable. A new framework is introduced to address this, incorporating concepts from submodular function optimization. This allows us to offer the first non-trivial regret analysis for combinatorial experts subject to delays in a known distribution. Furthermore, our approach provides improved upper bounds for several delayed bandit scenarios, including when lost opportunities to play are taken into account. Additionally, our work introduces a linear bandit algorithm that is the first to offer non-trivial regret bounds in a delayed setting, with its performance based solely on the immediate reward. The analytical methods employed in this work can also be applied to other scenarios with phase-dependent delays, including when experts and bandits are combined.

Current text-generation algorithms in dialogue can be flawed. Specifically, optimizing task success using reinforcement learning alone often leads to low lexical diversity in task-oriented settings. The proposed reason is a lack of fundamental understanding of text-generation objectives and how they impact the learning process during model training. A novel theoretical framework has been developed for generating text in dialogue, comprising underlying language patterns and specific language uses that together produce contextually relevant and syntactically correct text. The framework leverages structural constraints to guide the creation of candidate utterances. The framework also introduces theoretical metrics for assessing diversity and semantic coherence in text generation, outperforming existing metrics in evaluation. The generated text is competitive with state-of-the-art models in task success and is also more natural according to human judgments. The framework is compatible with various objective functions, speaker models, and training techniques.

Following Quantum Chromodynamics' 1972 formulation, a breakthrough in its regularization came when Kenneth Wilson applied it to Euclidean lattices. This opened doors for in-depth numerical analyses of QCD's non-perturbative properties, albeit initially plagued by significant finite-size effects. The advent of QCD's lattice description marked the beginning of a new era, and subsequent advancements in algorithms and computational power have since made it possible to investigate QCD under both non-equilibrium conditions and in the presence of quark matter.
