We detail the reasoning behind implementing a quantum S-matrix framework for tackling classical gravitational scattering between two bodies. Furthermore, a method is briefly discussed for computing black hole metrics across multiple spatial dimensions.

We investigate the two- or three-dimensional Navier-Stokes equations defined within a bounded region. This model takes into account an external force that introduces instability and is constrained by no-slip boundary conditions. The goal of our work is to stabilize this system through finite dimensional feedback controls in the vicinity of an unstable equilibrium in critical Sobolev and Besov spaces that approximate L^3(Omega) in three dimensions. This research setting has substantial implications as the uncontrolled dynamics' well-posedness issue has been solved in the mentioned space quotient space in a seminal work by Chemin. By building upon her approach, we leverage generalized Strichartz estimates in Sobolev and Besov spaces that allow us to derive the existence of such localized feedback controls in the context of critical Besov spaces. This work presents a novel strategy that generalizes Chebotarevski-Lemari\'e-Chalonsie's work in smooth spaces and offers an efficient and innovative solution to stabilizing three-dimensional flows via localized feedback controls in the vicinity of an unstable equilibrium in the critical Sobolev and Besov spaces that approximate L^3(Omega).

Language learning dictionaries can facilitate vocabulary acquisition by supplying 
word definitions, although conventional dictionaries may struggle with 
capturing word meanings that vary across different contexts. A potential solution 
is introduced in this study: the LitMind Dictionary, an online dictionary platform 
accessible through a web interface. It can automatically produce a definition 
based on user-provided words and surrounding context. Furthermore, the LitMind 
Dictionary supports multilingual queries, enabling the generation of definitions 
for Chinese and English, as well as cross-language inquiries between these two 
languages. A simplified user interface enables quick comprehension of query terms 
and enhances the overall user experience. The LitMind Dictionary is open-source, 
and the code, as well as data used in its development, are openly available on 
GitHub.

The growing interest in transparent AI has led to an increase in research on explainable recommendation systems. Among these, post-hoc methods have been identified as the most practical solutions for intricate models that operate as "black-boxes." Recent studies have exposed limitations in local surrogate-based post-hoc explanations regarding their inherent reliability, especially in critical applications such as human-centric recommendation tasks. Moreover, an ideal explanation should enhance key aspects of user experience including clarity and trustworthiness, posing additional challenges to the current approaches. However, a classical post-hoc model utilizing surrogates demonstrates dependence on the model itself, thus falling short in guaranteeing the accuracy of generated explanations.

Quantum devices based on superconducting properties may be effectively produced
using semiconductor-superconductor hybrids, consisting of materials in close
contact and a well-coupled interface. The efficiency of these hybrid quantum
circuits could significantly improve with thermally stable, directly connected
structures like in situ grown quantum wells. The electronic characteristic of
these quantum wells needs to be maintained due to an established electronic
connection with the superconductor. We examine near-surface InAs/GaAs quantum
wells grown using molecular beam epitaxy to understand the relationship between
their interface properties and an inherent effect known as Fermi level pinning.
The pinning level's position stabilizes the hybrid material's electronic interface
properties, resulting in consistent low-minimum tunneling density of states. The
Fermi level positioning at the InAs surface can be controlled through introduced
surface defects that act as electrical charges. The placement of these defects near
the surface distorts the surrounding surface charges and alters pinning levels. As
a result, these surface defects offer a viable approach to adjusting the tunnel
barrier width, crucial for hybrid material optimization in application to
superconducting circuits.

Research has shown that certain distributional assumptions are required to guarantee the reliable learnability of complex concepts when evaluating a robust model's accuracy and applying local queries such as membership queries. We examine the requirements for learning a robust model through both membership queries and membership/query queries, and find that robust concept learnability becomes feasible with either type of query alone given a suitable distributional assumption. This investigation highlights the practical implications of two robust learning assumptions - the Restricted Isometry Property (RIP) and Restricted Lipschitz Envelope (RLE) - and the greater adaptability offered by query queries in reducing the necessary level of distributional control (or "smoothness"). Specifically, we show that robust concept learnability is feasible with very low-level smoothness when using query queries, whereas having roughly the same requirement when using membership queries. Also, we show that robust concept learnability is feasible under much weaker conditions when the learner is allowed to use classification responses (query attacks), whereas having larger requirements for the same condition when just using membership queries. These findings emphasize the robustness adversarial resistance offered by each type of query and the lower requirement for the distribution to be "smooth."

Our previous research significantly sped up Sinkhorn iteration by taking advantage of a kernel matrix's inherent properties, transforming the most time-consuming step of the algorithm. This time, we've analyzed the kernel matrix's underlying structure and moved in a different direction, exploiting its triangular pattern. The breakthrough finding that a kernel matrix is inherently triangular when specific positive scaling is applied has allowed us to develop an entirely new formulation of Sinkhorn's problem. This new approach uses a linear solver that is both efficient and versatile, and we have successfully recreated the kernel matrix's properties after each iteration. As a result, our proposed algorithm outperforms the standard Sinkhorn method by two orders of magnitude in terms of computational speed. Notably, our Fast Sinkhorn II solution is simple, extending existing code with minimal additions, and fully compatible with OpenCV's widely adopted Sinkhorn implementation.

Young stars emitting intense X-ray and UV radiation can drastically alter planetary atmospheres, influencing both mass loss and chemistry. Observing AU Mic, an active 22-million-year-old star hosting two planets inside its debris disk, presents an extraordinary chance to study these impacts in relation to age and orbital distance. Our study entails over five hours of Hubble Space Telescope observations of AU Mic's Far-UV spectrum and X-ray data from the XMM-Newton telescope during a flare and in quiescence, supplemented with 20 flares detected in the U and X bands. Analyzing AU Mic's spectrum yielded Far-UV flux measurements of 3.2 x 10^26 and 6.1 x 10^26 photons s^-1, corresponding to quiescence and flare activity, respectively, likely emanating from the star's outer atmosphere. Our findings also infer a UV luminosity of approximately 3.2 x 10^31 erg s^-1, within the range proposed for AU Mic b and c, suggesting they might have more resistant atmospheres than previously thought. Nonetheless, intense stellar radiation could eventually cause these exoplanets to lose mass.

We develop an innovative approach to describe the friction caused by radiation experienced by particles moving through a medium with mechanical resistance. We introduce an effect where the medium is warped by the motion of charged particles in a way that the Larmor formula accurately describes the energy lost due to radiation. We compare this description to a different model that has been suggested by other researchers and find that both versions work similarly, but the new approach seems more straightforward and easy to work with. We also think our method could be easily extended to more complex situations, including cases where the medium is at an angle to the direction of charged particles moving through it.

In the context of an unevenly distributed classification problem, most popular classifiers are known to favor larger groups, and the nearest neighbor classifier is not immune to this phenomenon. This issue is addressed in a newly proposed statistical framework for the nearest neighbor classification method, which handles datasets where the majority classes outweigh minority ones. Initially developed for binary classification problems, this method is extended to accommodate multiple classes. Unlike existing over-sampling techniques that involve generating fake data points, this method achieves replicable results by sidestepping pseudo observation generation. Moreover, this method has demonstrated Bayesian risk consistency when subjected to relevant conditions and shows significant improvement in its performance compared to other existing methods, all backed up by a comprehensive analysis of several reference datasets.

We employ photometry data from multiple sources to identify ultra-bright Quasi-Stellar Objects (QSOs) located at distant regions of space. By utilizing SkyMapper's DR3, along with 2MASS, VHS, and other datasets, we combine them with accurate positions from Gaia DR2 and eDR3. As a result, we successfully discover 142 new Southern QSOs between 4.7 and 6.1 billion light-years away, along with further 25 previously identified QSOs within this range, which are then fitted to the latest QSO luminosity function. We find that the luminosity density of QSOs at z = 5.0 increases by 60% and the volume density at z = 5.5 rises by 25.4% compared to previous studies by Tyndall et al. and through an extrapolation of the function, we establish a lower bound for the cosmic density of massive ( > 10^9 M_\odot) stars at z > 5. However, we also observe a discrepancy in the predicted and actual QSO luminosity functions at z > 5.5, indicating the presence of an additional, yet unknown source of luminosity at z ~ 5.5.

We have successfully observed the charge-tunneling phenomenon occurring between a quantum dot and a superconducting island using a technique that employs radio-frequency sensing. Our approach has allowed us to distinguish between different types of tunneling events, specifically those driven by individual particles as well as by pairs of particles called Cooper pairs. Furthermore, we've found that the quantum dot can be utilized to detect changes in the superconductor's electronic state without needing traditional electrical current measurements, providing us with insight into previously inaccessible subgap energy states. Our findings offer valuable insights for future research focused on detecting parity-dependent interactions between these two key components.

Our research explores the contraction behavior of specific types of shockwaves in systems of equations, particularly those that conserve quantities, given the presence of a convex "stability" function. To expand upon existing theories, we introduce a new concept: complete inflexibility, which is established for systems of two equations and various types of "quasi-conservative" systems, such as those found in gas mixtures. Additionally, we identify a broad class of systems that satisfy a specific stability condition and in which shockwaves exhibit contraction behavior when the stability function lies within a particular range.

We explore novel view generation -- the challenge of generating distant, unseen views by virtually navigating a given image -- through a new, promising approach. Our contribution is DiffDreamer, an unsupervised system that synthesizes novel long-distance views by training on just a single image, without the need for extensive training datasets or camera parameters. Our results indicate that it significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art methods by producing views with higher detail and accuracy in both qualitative and quantitative assessments.

Many complex systems feature networks where interactions between diverse agents combine simple local rules to create complex emergent behaviors. While recent research has found connections between network structure and the underlying dynamic processes, detecting random complex patterns remains a pressing challenge. We develop a new, straightforward method grounded in mathematical techniques to discover and manage complex patterns that arise on large-scale networks, even without prior knowledge of their structure. This approach identifies underlying dynamics by analyzing a collection of snapshots representing network states over time. By applying operator-theoretic methods, it converts complex patterns into a linear format, facilitating model predictive control. We show that our proposed method simplifies a complex problem typically difficult to solve in large networks, transforming it into a more tractable and efficient optimization problem with a reduced number of variables.

The dynamics of a liquid film on a fiber heavily depend on the boundary conditions at the liquid-solid interface. This understanding has led to a theoretical model that uses the axisymmetric Stokes equations to examine the effect of slip at the liquid-solid interface on the Rayleigh-Plateau instability. The new theoretical model predicts that the onset of instability occurs at a lower flow rate when the liquid film is thin enough for slip conditions to apply, and this instability rate increases with the level of slip efficiency. Moreover, our results suggest that certain types of slip conditions can lead to a distinctive instability pattern that could facilitate the formation of liquid threads from a fiber coated with a thin liquid film.

We investigate the temporal Lipschitz stability for solutions of the Hunter-Saxton equation, focusing on $\alpha$-dissipative solutions with $\alpha$ a constant in the interval $[0,1]$. We introduce and study the properties of metrics both in the Lagrangian and Eulerian frameworks to determine Lipschitz stability within those systems.

Evaluating scoliosis with ultrasound imaging is particularly difficult for individuals without visual contact to the spine. A reliable and consistent method for accurately assessing scoliosis would be beneficial for those with visual impairments. A study presented an advanced ultrasound system employing a robotic scanner that enables automatic spine tracking and reliable vertebral identification. The purpose of this research was to compare the accuracy of scoliosis assessments obtained through both manual and robotic ultrasound methods. Ten healthy subjects with scoliosis were evaluated by two physical therapists who respectively used both manual and robotic scanning techniques. Scoliosis angles were then determined through ultrasound, X-ray, and radiographic examinations. The results revealed that robotic scanning produced scoliosis angles that correlated well with those obtained through X-ray and radiographic examinations, with mean biases and coefficients of variation being similar for both manual and robotic scanning. Furthermore, the scoliosis angles obtained through robotic scanning were found to be more precise and consistent than those acquired through manual scanning. The study's findings suggest the robotic scanning method as a more trustworthy approach for assessing scoliosis, particularly in cases where repeated measurements are essential. A potential application of this technology is to develop a portable device that would enable individuals with visual impairments to independently assess their scoliosis and maintain track of changes over time.

This paper introduces an innovative method for duration modelling in statistical parametric speech synthesis by training a recurrent model to predict phone transition probabilities frame-by-frame. Unlike traditional approaches that rely on specific distribution types and mean durations for synthesis, this new approach can generate synthetic durations for novel utterances based on median duration estimates for novel phone combinations. Since duration modelling is specifically tailored to synthesis, this method abolishes the need for a prior likelihood estimate, making it suitable for conversational speech synthesis. Furthermore, this method's performance is demonstrated through its application in the CSLT Japanese speech database, and the results show a substantial improvement in duration modelling when compared to a parametric approach using Gaussian mixtures and non-parametric duration modelling that directly predicts quantised duration values in Mandarin Mandarin.

Identifying online hate speech is increasingly critical due to its capacity to inflict emotional and psychological harm on minority groups. A recent study from TU Berlin's research team analyzed the performance of different Natural Language Processing models on subtasks one and two of the 2021 Indo-European language shared task, which focused on detecting hate speech and derogatory content. Our team assessed the effectiveness of models that rely on word and character-based recurrent neural networks and those employing transfer learning via BERT, all of which utilized a shared task dataset. It was discovered that models employing transfer learning outperformed others across both tasks.

Multi-input multi-output (MIMO) networks attempt to improve ensemble performance by training separate subnetworks within a base model and combining their predictions. However, these networks have been found to inefficiently use parameters, hindering their adoption on constrained devices such as smartphones and AR/VR devices. This study suggests that a key issue with current feature sharing methods lies in their randomized approach to assigning individual subnetworks to data inputs. To address this, we introduce a synchronous feature sharing framework, which synchronously divides the input data among the base model's channels. Our proposed framework is theoretically justified and its performance is empirically validated across various datasets, resulting in consistent reductions of up to 50% in parameters, while also achieving comparable to improved ensemble performance.

This study undertakes a comprehensive analysis of existing datasets pertinent to the analysis of historical documents through image-based techniques. Specifically, this involves exploring collections of handwritten manuscripts and early printed materials. Acquiring reliable datasets, facilitating the advancement of research in this field, this survey offers a vital reference point by providing a detailed review of currently available datasets that are Adams-based, providing first-time insights into their creation methodologies, and highlighting their respective applications.

Due to the inherent elasticity in their design, industrial robots that lack advanced precision-enhancing technology are only marginally effective for machining tasks. Besides issues related to structure, temperature, and support bearings, one major factor behind elasticity is the backlash in the transmission systems. This study proposes a method for improving trajectory precision using supplementary sensors and a novel feedback control strategy in combination with a feed-forward approach based on flatness. For this purpose, a novel forward feed-back control algorithm is introduced, which relies on supplementary position sensors placed near the drive to accurately track the true system displacement. This innovative approach combines with a forward feed-forward control method, which utilizes supplementary sensors as a displacement compensation tool, significantly enhancing the precision of industrial robots with transmission-induced elasticity. This solution, which only requires the addition of simple, cost-effective supplementary sensors to existing industrial robots, offers an efficient means to improve precision. Moreover, it has the potential to optimize the robot through parameter estimation and the design of a flatness-based reference trajectory.

The study of how chronic diseases evolve throughout an individual's lifetime has primarily been based on an environmental perspective. However, there's been growing interest in incorporating lifestyle and other behavioral factors into this analysis. An analytical framework known as Multiple State Analysis (MSA) provides a framework for examining these multiple factors, along with their interconnections. Although MSA has been utilized in a few earlier studies, there is still a need for a more detailed explanation of how to incorporate specific covariates, including life-style factors, into the model. An additional requirement for incorporating lifestyle factors is access to extensive, long-term data on relevant variables. Such data is available through electronic health records (EHR). Our research utilized a large dataset of myocardial infarction patients and their health histories to better understand how health changes over time and how different factors contribute to this change. An important extension to the MSA model allowed it to accommodate the analysis of health patterns leading up to a specific event, in this case, myocardial infarction. An accompanying article provides supplementary information on the model, including a detailed description of the variables used in the analysis and access to the associated R code.

One widely accepted method for evaluating electronic integrals in complex molecules involves a modified version of Becke's partitioning scheme, originally designed for functions that decline rapidly over distance. This method employs overlapping grids at each atomic site, effectively dividing the integrand. Although the unaltered Becke scheme exhibits slow convergence when applied to free electronic states found in processes like photoionization, this modified version achieves efficient results comparable to those for bound electronic states. To accomplish this, the modified scheme incorporates a unique transition mechanism where atomic weights are gradually deactivated at a distance of a few bond lengths from their respective atomic nuclei and replaced by a smoothly converging weight that tends toward unity. Following this method, the integrals associated with atomic sites are calculated using smaller spherical grids, while the interstitial regions' residual integrals are calculated with a central grid. Unnecessary calculations associated with unphysical overshooting at atomic nuclei, found in the original scheme, are thus eliminated. A unique interpolation method is also developed to effectively combine local and multipole expansions in the interstitial grid. The proposed scheme is shown to effectively evaluate both Gaussian and Slater-type orbitals. Furthermore, the method is successfully applied to evaluate electronic integrals in simulations of high-luminosity synchrotron radiation-induced photoionization in water.

In a graph, a subset of vertices forms a resolving set if, for any two vertices, a single set vertex is positioned at different distances from the two vertices. The problem of finding a resolving set of size at most k, called the Metric Dimension problem, has been a subject of research since the 1970s. The problem was found to be NP-hard, with parameterization by the vertex cover number yielding fixed-parameter tractability. However, the complexity under different parameters remained unclear until our recent discovery, where the problem was found to be W[1]-hard when parameterized by the feedback vertex set number. Additionally, we found that parameterization by the vertex cover number results in the problem not admitting a polynomial kernel unless a specific hypothesis is true, while parameterization by the distance to cluster vertex cover does not admit a polynomial kernel unless a specific hypothesis is true. Our results contribute to an understanding of the computational complexity of graph problems by incorporating structural graph theory parameters.

Domain theory's powerdomains hold significant importance in the semantics of non-deterministic programming languages.  This paper extends powerdomains to directed spaces - a concept equivalent to T_0 monotone-determined spaces.  Powerdomain-like spaces (upper, lower, and convex powerspaces) of directed spaces are defined through free algebras, and it is shown that these spaces correspond to specialized powerdomains.  Notably, it is proven that these spaces are equivalent for CEs and that they fail to be equivalent for general directed spaces.  The study also reveals that upper, lower, and convex powerspaces do not have equivalent lifting and powerlift properties within the framework of directed spaces.

Past and potential future Earth climate states have included extremely warm 'hothouse' environments with unknown atmospheric behavior, characterized by a distinctive low atmospheric heating pattern. In contrast to typical cooling effects, 'hothouse' climates are distinguished by a blocked window region for water vapor, which has led to theories of resulting temperature inversions and altered cloud formations. Prior climate modeling has failed to resolve turbulent air motions and cloud dynamics directly, leaving significant gaps in understanding hothouse climate processes. In this research, simulations resolving convection explicitly found that 'hothouse' low atmospheric heating shifts the water cycle from steady state to a periodic regime, characterized by intense precipitation and long dry spells. The transition to this regime was associated with increased local precipitation and cloud cover, along with a positive climate feedback that may stabilize 'hothouse' environments. The research implies the presence of a new type of temporal atmospheric self-organization, affecting both cloud formations and erosion in hothouse climates.

We've established an inverse Penrose transform for self-dual Yang-Mills theory and its spin-off variants in a flat space environment. The spin-off variant's twistor action fits within the broader BF framework. When we deviated from the standard self-dual sector of this variant, we stumbled upon a novel action describing higher-spin Yang-Mills theory, an expansion of Yang-Mills theory itself. This theory's twistor action builds directly upon Yang-Mills theory's original form.

The application of deep neural networks in medical image classification has shown great promise due to their advanced image mapping capabilities. Despite this, current deep learning-based methods rely heavily on a vast quantity of high-quality, labeled images which often contains errors. Consequently, developing robust training techniques that minimize the negative effects of noisy labels is of the utmost importance for achieving optimal model performance. To address this challenge, we propose an innovative method based on Bayesian statistics called the BLRM that prevents DNNs from overfitting noisy images. By leveraging MAP probability and an exponentially time-dependent function to characterize noise likelihood, the BLRM effectively distinguishes between noisy and legitimate image labels during the training process. Additionally, the proposed method utilizes a straightforward statistical model to estimate the posterior probability distribution of each image label, allowing Bayesian statistics to accurately infer the likelihood that a given image label is accurate. Experimental results on diverse medical image datasets have demonstrated that the proposed BLRM method effectively mitigates the negative consequences of noisy data and achieves superior performance even with severely noisy images. The proposed BLRM's performance is compared with state-of-the-art noise-resistant deep learning-based methods on various medical image classification tasks, such as multi-organ abdominal analysis and retina lesion detection. The source code of the proposed BLRM will be publicly available to facilitate its practical use.

Consider a unit cube, $Q_n$, in $n$-dimensional space and a function space, $C(Q_n)$, consisting of continuous functions from $Q_n$ to $\mathbb{R}$. Define the norm of a function as its maximum absolute value over $Q_n$. Let $\Pi_1\left(\mathbb{R}^n\right)$ be the set of polynomials of degree at most one, i.e., linear functions on $\mathbb{R}^n$. An interpolation projector $P: C(Q_n) \to \Pi_1\left(\mathbb{R}^n\right)$ maps a function to its best least-squares approximation in $C(Q_n)$ with respect to some norm. This work estimates the norm of $P$ for functions that have a Lipschitz constant, $\lambda$.

A correlated random walk (CRW) is derived from the Grover matrix, the evolution matrix of the Grover walk on a graph G, and an explicit formula is given for the characteristic polynomial of the CRW's transition probability matrix, utilising a generalized zeta function related to the graph's Betti numbers. This is exemplified in the cases of triangular, hypercube, and rook graphs. Additionally, the paper investigates statistical properties of the CRW on these graph classes.

In a total functions logic such as HOL, certain non-terminating functions are difficult to define directly. To overcome this limitation, a clock mechanism is often introduced to enforce termination after a specified evaluation depth. While commonly regarded as cumbersome, we argue that alternative methods of adding a clock exist, with varying levels of intrusion. We present a new approach that simplifies termination proofs without overly utilizing the clock mechanism, particularly illustrated through the context of functional big-step semantics for programming language interpretations.

The accuracy of models predicting the spatial and temporal characteristics of wall-bounded instantaneously flowing water is heavily reliant on the accurately portrayed occurrence of coherent patterns. For this, a system that simulates the patterns in a specific confined wall-bounded flow is used, with a unique wall pattern prediction model developed using data from a highly detailed simulation. By combining this pattern prediction model with a solution to the fluid dynamics of the system, a comprehensive model of the flow is established, which effectively replicates the flow in different scenarios. With this model, a comprehensive comparison of the effects of different pattern occurrences is possible, which can lead to a better understanding of the effects of this pattern on the flow in practical situations. Moreover, this model facilitates the simulation of this flow in scenarios where there is no data available, which can provide valuable insights in situations where this type of simulation isn't possible with current methods.

This study demonstrates the presence of self-dual (topological) solitons within a modified baby Skyrme model that incorporates Born-Infeld term governed gauge field behavior. The effective implementation of the Bogomol'nyi-Prasad-Sommerfield framework yields an energy lower bound, with corresponding self-dual equations whose solutions manifest as the limiting solitons that achieve this bound. The lower bound on energy, known as the Bogomol'nyi bound, exhibits proportionality to the topological charge of the Skyrme field, thereby being quantized. Conversely, the overall magnetic flux is a nonquantized entity. Additionally, this model may be generalized to include composite matter fields, encompassing either fermions or bosons, within its comprehensive framework.

For a three-dimensional Weyl semimetal model in a magnetic field, where each unit cell has an orbital magnetic flux of $p/q$ with $1\le p \le q$, we analyze its phase diagram. When $p$ exceeds $p_c$ with $p_c = 2$ in the limit of large $q$, a semimetallic phase gives way to a fully insulating phase, where $p_c$ is independent of $q$ in the limit of large $q$. The breaking point of the phase transition is accurate to a leading-order effect of $1/q$. Our results apply to a specific electron model interacting with a local spin in a system of periodic boundaries. The phase diagram also includes the existence of a time-reversal-broken phase, where this phase can be identified at $p=2$ with $q$ being large.

This research paper introduces an advanced optical nanoantenna design, consisting of a hybrid silicon nanoring coupled with a localised assembly of quantum dots, which together constitute an efficient source of unidirectional photons when subjected to optical stimulation. The structure features a narrow 10-nanometer gap separating a gold mirror from the nanoring and quantum dots, enabling efficient interaction between the quantum dots and the dual modes supported by the setup - resonant gap modes and radiative antenna modes. Our experimental findings confirm that the quantum dots within the nanogap can efficiently couple to these modes to enhance the absorption of the stimulating light and emit light with high directionality. Furthermore, we demonstrate that adjusting simple geometric parameters, such as the nanoring's central hole, allows us to independently tune the resonance spectral positions of the setup. This unique structure offers a promising platform for the efficient and directional emission of single photons, offering significant potential for applications in quantum information physics and photonic operations.

Mechanical screening, a widely recognized phenomenon, is utilized across solids and fluids to obstruct small particle movement.  A 2008 theoretical study proposed an unconventional approach, known as anomalous screening, which suggests that small particles encounter increased resistance closer to larger particles due to mechanical interactions, resulting in an unusual, potentially contradictory screening mechanism.  Verifying this theory through experiments has been challenging due to its non-bosonic nature and the difficulties in isolating the system from external influences.  Our research successfully demonstrates the existence of anomalous screening by isolating individual grains from external influences and measuring force interactions at the nanoscale, complemented by numerical simulations which confirm that standard screening theories fail to block very small particles.  Additionally, our findings show that anomalous screening occurs through mechanical coupling between constituents and the potential existence of a critical size limit where blocking efficiency declines with increasing particle size.  A comprehensive analysis of granular screening suggests that mechanical blocking efficiency decreases in a logarithmic pattern with particle size.

Utilizing first-principles calculations, our research involves analyzing silicene in relation to hexagonal boron nitride substrates. Hexagonal boron nitride, being a semiconductor, has weaker interactions with silicene in comparison to metallic substrates. As a result, silicene's band gap can potentially be expanded up to 50 meV. Additionally, the impact of manganese decoration on the system is explored by calculating the onsite Hubbard interaction parameter, which significantly differs between decoration at the top and hollow sites. Furthermore, the system's induced magnetism is thoroughly examined.

The Sgr A East supernova remnant, located near the center of the Milky Way, poses a mystery with age estimates ranging from extremely young, around 1-2 thousand years, to a significantly older, 10 thousand year estimate. Our objective is to create a straightforward simulation of a supernova rembubble expanding at the speed of a young supernova remnant and using straightforward methods to estimate its age. Our simulations indicate that a supernova exploding about 500 parsecs from the Galactic center, with an energy equivalent to one solar mass worth of kinetic energy, would produce a similar shape and size of remubble that matches the observed Sgr A East shape and size within 10 thousand years. Therefore, it is most likely that Sgr A East is the remains of a young supernova, with estimates suggesting the supernova occurred around 1.5 thousand years ago to 10 thousand years ago. Additionally, our findings imply that the central black hole played little to no role in the expansion of the remubble and that pressure from surrounding material, known as the "outside-in" model, is the most likely explanation for the expansion of Sgr A East rather than another proposed model involving the interaction with nearby H II regions.

The study examines various oversampling methods to classify multi-class topics, particularly focusing on the performance of SMOTE, a popular method for generating new samples based on minority class examples, and its two variants along with random oversampling in text classification tasks. The research assesses the efficiency of SMOTE, its Borderline and ADASYN modifications, and random oversampling in conjunction with machine learning algorithms such as k-nearest neighbor, support vector machine, and different types of neural networks, using text representations. The outcomes suggest that using oversampling methods enhances the accuracy of classification and indicates that the performance of KNN and SVM algorithms is heavily influenced by class imbalance issues, whereas neural networks show resilience against it.

This study analyzes data from an online monitoring system of U.S. local news to explore connections between COVID coverage, regional case and death rates, and characteristics of news outlets and their audiences. Using a distinct dataset of over 750,000 articles from over 300 outlets between April 2020 and February 2021, our results show that local news outlets initially covered COVID at a rate influenced by national death rates but ultimately became less correlated as other issues like the U.S. elections dominated headlines. Additionally, our research reveals that local news COVID coverage varied based on the area's politics, news outlet popularity, and audience size, and also indicates that disadvantaged populations received less pandemic-related information.

Smoothed particle hydrodynamics possesses innate conservation capabilities, which remain flawless when accurately integrated, maintaining machine-precise levels of total mass, energy, and linear/angular momentum conservation. Notably, this property holds significant value in computational astrophysics for processes such as binary interactions and compact object mergers. The standard SPH implementation, which incorporates a form of density estimation based on smoothing kernels, has been found to slightly distort momentum conservation due to inaccurately calculated density estimates, which differ from the actual densities according to the continuity equation. While such inaccuracies are minimal in static conditions, they are pronounced in dynamic scenarios. To rectify this deficiency, this paper presents the implementation of a novel, density-based form of the continuity equation that ensures precise conservation of linear and angular momentum using the Fast Multipole Method. A comprehensive set of test cases is presented, which showcases the implementation's ability to conserve momentum with a precision of -2e-12 units.

Numerical studies have been conducted on the JLab Hall A Experimental Program's data, focusing on the $\vec {p}$-$e$ transfer of polarization in the $Q^2$ range between 1 and 4 GeV$^2$.  This research examined how the final proton's polarization, resulting from the $G_{M} / G_{E}$ ratio measurement, is affected by $e$-$e'$ correlations, as well as by polarization transfer from the initial proton.  Specifically, our findings reveal a roughly 60% connection between the final proton's polarization and the initial proton's polarization.  Additionally, our findings illustrate a prominent impact of the $G_{M} / G_{E}$ ratio on the proton's polarization, which in turn highlights the importance of considering $e$-$e'$ correlations in the ratio's determination.

We develop a novel, yet efficient, method for augmenting existing data to enhance the learning capacity of reinforcement and imitation learning from experienced models. The policy cloning approach, a fundamental component of various learning techniques, is our focus, as it leverages the expertise of a guiding model to shape a student model's behavior. In order to accomplish this, we implement our proposed method, augmented policy cloning, which introduces artificially generated states to a training environment, making the system sensitive to its surroundings, thus greatly reducing the gap between the student and guiding models. Our results demonstrate that augmented policy cloning significantly shortens the amount of time needed for a model to converge, in addition to keeping the student model's behavior similar to that of the experienced model.

A comprehensive study of the creation of two Higgs bosons ($hh$) paired with a vector boson ($W$ or $Z$) using a massive dataset of 139 inverse femtobarns of proton collisions at a 13 TeV energy has been carried out utilizing the ATLAS detector at the Large Hadron Collider. The research explores final states in which the vector boson decays into electrons and neutrinos or into electrons and other electrons and neutrinos, and each Higgs boson decays into pairs of $b$-quarks. It aims to find these pair productions along with predicted backgrounds and determine an observed limit on the product of cross-sections is given in terms of the coupling of the Higgs bosons to each other. The results also illustrate a 72% alignment of the expected observations with the standard model, both in the case of the vector boson decaying into electrons and neutrinos and in the case of the vector boson decaying into electrons and other electrons and neutrinos. Furthermore, the results of the sensitivity of the results have been applied to restrict heavily coupled Higgs bosons in the framework of two coupled Higgs models and the results of the results have been particularly useful in understanding the properties of the Higgs boson in the standard model in the context of the field.

Atomic magnetometers that utilize self-oscillating technology and driven by resonant modulation, pass modulated light through a collection of cesium atoms to produce a stable frequency modulation pattern. The maser signal is generated when light interacts with the atoms, resulting in a break in modulation and forming a distinctive "sideband" pattern on the frequency spectrum. The stability of this system depends on its ability to function as a traditional maser. We investigate the phenomenon where inter-atomic interactions cause fluctuations in the system, leading to a loss of coherence and mapping these into a detectable sideband pattern. The study provides insight into how quantum fluctuations affect atomic systems, providing an opportunity to observe Rabi sinking in a digital context.

For K3 surfaces with an automorphism having a Siegel disk, the associated Picard number falls between $0$ and $18$ and must be an even integer. Conversely, applying the technique of hypergeometric groups, K3 surface automorphisms possessing Siegel disks can be constructed to demonstrate all conceivable Picard numbers through the identification and computation of relevant algebraic numbers derived from Lefschetz-type formulas and their corresponding residues.

A supergravity unified framework neutralino is proposed as a plausible candidate for dark matter, where a long-lived neutralino decays into the hidden sector's lightest supersymmetric particle, exceeding the age of the universe. We introduce an extension to the MSSM/SUGRA model with a $U(1)_{X_1} \times U(1)_{X_2}$ hidden sector gauge sector, where the hidden sector neutralino is lighter than its visible counterpart, leading to a loop-suppressed radiative decay process. The computation demonstrates that the visible sector neutralino can decay with a lifetime greater than the age of the universe. The detectability of this scenario lies in the indirect observation of a signature decay product into the hidden sector neutralino accompanied by a high-energy gamma ray photon, accessible through Fermi-LAT and future SKA, CTA experiments. Several benchmarks showcasing suppressed hadronic annihilation channels are also introduced and cross-checked against existing limits from AMS-02 and Fermi-LAT to ensure compliance with experimental constraints on long-lived particles and gamma ray emissions.

The main contributions of this study include developing an Efficient Polynomial-Time Approximation Scheme for finding the minimum surface topography (genus and non-orientable genus) for complex network graphs that are densely connected. Densely connected networks are defined by a minimum edge count greater than some positive constant value relative to the number of vertices squared. Although a simple, constant factor approximation method exists for this graph class, providing high-precision approximations near 1:1 ratios required in genetics research and combinatorial mathematics has been difficult. Our study introduces a method that can be scaled up from a previous linear-time solution first described by Fabrizio Zanotti O'Neale, which was later built upon by Mader in 1993. In the course of our study, we demonstrated that our initial approach could also be applied to other graph surface topography problems to yield improved approximation rates.

A stochastic Newton algorithm for distributed convex optimization tasks is proposed, which utilizes individual machine capabilities to calculate gradient and Hessian-vector products for the same shared objective between communication intervals, significantly minimizing required communication rounds. Convergence analysis and performance preservation are demonstrated for quasi-self-concordant objectives like logistic regression, backed by empirical results.

Our approach to training a neural network to identify hate-speech in Hindi and Bengali is outlined in this work. We investigate the viability of leveraging transfer learning for these languages due to their shared origin, which lends them a degree of similarity. Our experiment's implementation on low-powered hardware yields results that hold up against those of more costly models, a noteworthy finding. Additionally, given the limited training data and our unfamiliarity with these languages, our study represents an attempt to decipher languages often shrouded in mystery.

In nuclear and particle physics, being able to identify the direction of nuclear recoils is a significant advantage. This capability, achieved at minimal cost, allows researchers to effectively remove electromagnetic background noise originating from beta decays or Cosmics-Ray Simulations when analyzing Dark Matter experiments. Fortunately, this is made possible due to the properties of drift-charged ions in the gas of Time Projection Chambers, which effectively act as markers indicating the path of recoiling nuclei. This concept is known as Direct Recoil Identification, DRI for short. By utilizing a device called the ProtoByrd TPC, operating at atmospheric pressure with 90% Ar/10% CO2, the effectiveness of DRI has been tested in various conditions. This study examines three different methods to achieve direct recoil identification: using the length of drift-charged ion paths, differences in electron ionization degrees along the path of the recoiling nucleus, and the time delay between the two types of paths. The results indicate that all three methods are viable means of identifying directional recoil information at atmospheric pressures in Dark Matter experiments.

A comprehensive set of rules governs the assessment of commercial drivers, with specific emphasis on the responsibility of drivers in vehicle maintenance. As the application of technological systems in driver evaluation becomes more widespread, there is a growing need to ensure these systems make decisions that are fair and consistent. However, even technologically advanced decision support systems have limitations in their ability to fully consider a driver's situation, and can therefore provide inaccurate vehicle condition assessments. Consequently, a decision support system's outputs are likely to be more reliable when moderated by human experts who possess invaluable knowledge and industry understanding. Moderation also offers several benefits, as it allows for individual circumstances to be taken into account, fair and unbiased decision-making, and enhanced trust due to increased transparency in the decision-making process. Moderation can be implemented through a simple process that involves reviewing and adjusting decisions made by technological systems. By analyzing the effects of moderation on driver evaluation, we investigate its potential impact on the decision-making process and its application in facilitating informed decisions. Our findings highlight the importance of moderation in ensuring the fairness of technological systems in making decisions.

This paper reports on the findings from the Out-Of-Vocabulary (OOV) track of the
Speaker reID V2 challenge. The track focused on addressing speaker identification
issues related to unseen speakers, short speeches, and missing input speeches. The
challenge's impact on model performance was thoroughly examined from multiple
angles, with conclusions drawn about the optimal approach for setting challenge and
Evaluating model performance in these scenarios. The track's details, including
the dataset used, evaluation methods, experimental design, and results, are presented.
The accompanying code is available at https://github.com/igniteech/oov-track-reidv2.

Random fields in mathematical models depict how interconnected random variables behave over time, influencing a variety of disciplines from statistical physics to system biology. Since their introduction in the 19th century, little has been known about the link between their dynamic behaviors and geometric properties of the underlying spaces they're defined within. To address this gap, a numerical method was proposed for determining geodesic distances in Gaussian random field manifolds, involving two main components: deriving the underlying metric (a specific first-order matrix), and computing the necessary Christoffel symbols from the derived system. These calculations are used to solve the resulting system of differential equations through iterative approaches, such as Runge-Kutta. When applied to different scenarios, this method demonstrated its capability to estimate distances while also uncovering intriguing results where reversed geodesic curves exhibited distinct patterns from the originals, hinting at possible irreversible geometric changes within moving references following specific trajectories.
In our research, we conduct experiments on Rayleigh-Taylor Instability by introducing a controlled disturbance through magnetic levitation technology.

For a cuspidal Hecke eigenform $F$ attached to the symplectic group $Sp_n(Z)$ and a Dirichlet character $\chi$, we examine the standard twisted L-function, $L(s,F,\chi,St)$, and show that its algebraic component at critical point $m$ has bounded denominators as $\chi$ changes. This work refines a previous finding of Boecherer. A similar result also holds for the product of Hecke L-functions of primitive forms from the special linear group $SL_2(Z)$.

In a tight binding model using the non-equilibrium Green's functions formalism, researchers explored how spin-dependent transport behaves in armchair graphene nanoribbons with ferromagnetic gate control. The investigation delved into conductance and spin polarization oscillations caused by varying barrier heights, which can be regulated with gate voltages, in addition to analyzing the effects of varying widths on the band gap and contact nature.

This paper presents proofs of Korovkin theorem analogues in the realm of weakly nonlinear, monotone operators applied to multi-variable Banach lattices of functions. Our study encompasses the almost everywhere convergence, convergence in measure, and $L^{p}$-norm convergence. The discussion is supplemented by several examples that demonstrate the theoretical findings.

A graph on n vertices is called pancyclic if it contains a cycle of every possible length from 3 to n. In 1972, Erdos demonstrated that a graph on n vertices with n larger than 4k to the fourth power and an independence number of k will always contain all cycles. After his findings, he suggested the independence number squared should suffice. Many years later, in 2018, the conjecture was refined by Gerke, who proposed that an n-vertex graph with an independence number of k should contain cycles of length from 3 to n, provided n is sufficiently large in relation to k. A significant number of results have been achieved since 2018; however, the exact threshold at which the pancyclicity is achieved is still unknown and has been unresolved for over fifty years. In our investigation, we explored whether a certain threshold for n in relation to k exists. Upon re-examining Erdos' 1972 work, it becomes apparent that his work also addressed the problem of whether a graph with an independence number of k should also contain Hamiltonian cycles. In 1973, Sherk revealed that a required upper limit for the order of the graph, rather than the independence number, is applicable in Erdos' theorem. In contrast, in our investigation, we sought to determine whether a graph with an independence number of k contains not just all cycles but specifically Hamiltonian cycles.
